name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Atomic radius, oxidation states, and Lewis acidity

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding Group 13 elements:

Statement I: The atomic radius of gallium is smaller than that of aluminium due to the poor screening effect of the ten inner \(d\)-electrons in gallium.

Statement II: Down Group 13, the relative stability of the \(+1\) oxidation state increases in the order \(\mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Ga} < \mathrm{In} < \mathrm{Tl}\) because of the inert pair effect.

Statement III: Boron trifluoride (\(\mathrm{BF}_3\)) behaves as a Lewis base because the boron atom has six valence electrons and readily donates an electron pair.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Atomic Radius Trend in Group 13
On moving down Group 13 from aluminium (\(Z = 13\)) to gallium (\(Z = 31\)), ten \(3d\)-electrons are added to the inner core of gallium. Because \(d\)-orbitals have a diffuse shape, they offer poor shielding (screening) of the outer valence electrons from the increased nuclear charge. As a result, the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outer electrons in gallium increases, pulling them closer to the nucleus and making the atomic radius of gallium (\(135\ \mathrm{pm}\)) smaller than that of aluminium (\(143\ \mathrm{pm}\)). Hence, the claim regarding the smaller atomic radius of gallium compared to aluminium is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Stability of the \(+1\) Oxidation State
In heavier Group 13 elements, the intervening \(d\)- and \(f\)-orbitals poorly shield the valence \(ns^2\) electrons from the nuclear charge. Consequently, the \(ns^2\) electrons are held tightly and resist participation in bonding (the inert pair effect), leaving primarily the \(np^1\) electron available for bonding. Therefore, the stability of the \(+1\) oxidation state progressively increases down the group in the order \(\mathrm{Al} < \mathrm{Ga} < \mathrm{In} < \mathrm{Tl}\). Hence, the claim regarding the increasing stability of the \(+1\) oxidation state down Group 13 is correct.

Step 3: Application — Lewis Acid-Base Behaviour of \(\mathrm{BF}_3\)
In \(\mathrm{BF}_3\), boron forms three covalent bonds with fluorine and has only six electrons in its valence shell, making it an electron-deficient molecule with an incomplete octet. To achieve a stable octet configuration, \(\mathrm{BF}_3\) tends to accept a lone pair of electrons from electron-rich species (such as \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)). An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid, not a Lewis base. Hence, the claim that \(\mathrm{BF}_3\) behaves as a Lewis base is incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding the smaller atomic radius of gallium and the increasing stability of the \(+1\) oxidation state down Group 13 are both correct, whereas the claim describing \(\mathrm{BF}_3\) as a Lewis base is incorrect.

answer.text: Only Statement I and Statement III are correct
Only Statement I and Statement II are correct
Only Statement II and Statement III are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Properties of boric acid, diborane, and borax

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following three statements regarding important compounds of boron:

Statement I: Orthoboric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{BO}_3\)) is a weak monobasic acid that acts as a Lewis acid by accepting a hydroxyl ion (\(\mathrm{OH}^-\)) from water rather than releasing a proton directly.

Statement II: In diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)), all six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are identical two-centre two-electron bonds lying in a single plane.

Statement III: An aqueous solution of borax (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{B}_4\mathrm{O}_7\cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) is alkaline in nature because it hydrolyses in water to produce sodium hydroxide and orthoboric acid.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Acidic Nature of Orthoboric Acid
Orthoboric acid, \(\mathrm{B(OH)}_3\), is not a protonic acid because it does not ionise directly to release \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions on its own. Instead, boron has an incomplete octet and acts as a Lewis acid by accepting an electron pair from a hydroxyl ion (\(\mathrm{OH}^-\)) of water according to the equation \(\mathrm{B(OH)}_3 + 2\mathrm{HOH} \rightarrow [\mathrm{B(OH)}_4]^- + \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\). Because it accepts one \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) ion per molecule, it behaves as a weak monobasic Lewis acid. Hence, the claim regarding the acidic behaviour of orthoboric acid is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Structure and Bonding in Diborane
In diborane (\(\mathrm{B}_2\mathrm{H}_6\)), the two boron atoms and the four terminal hydrogen atoms lie in one plane, while the two bridging hydrogen atoms lie one above and one below this plane. The four terminal \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are normal two-centre two-electron (\(2\mathrm{c}-2\mathrm{e}\)) bonds, whereas the two bridging \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{B}\) bonds are three-centre two-electron (\(3\mathrm{c}-2\mathrm{e}\)) banana bonds. Therefore, not all six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds are identical or coplanar. Hence, the claim that all six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds in diborane are identical and coplanar is incorrect.

Step 3: Application — Hydrolysis of Borax
When borax dissolves in water, it undergoes hydrolysis according to the reaction \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{B}_4\mathrm{O}_7 + 7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH} + 4\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{BO}_3\). Since \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is a strong base and \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{BO}_3\) is a weak acid, the resulting aqueous solution is alkaline. Hence, the claim regarding the alkaline nature of aqueous borax is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding orthoboric acid acting as a weak monobasic Lewis acid and the alkaline nature of aqueous borax are correct, whereas the claim that all six \(\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds in diborane are identical and coplanar is incorrect.

answer.text: Only Statement I and Statement II are correct
Only Statement II and Statement III are correct
Only Statement I and Statement III are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Hydrolysis of tetrachlorides, carbon allotropes, and silicones

questiontext.text:
Examine the following three statements about Group 14 elements and their compounds:

Statement I: Unlike \(\mathrm{CCl}_4\), \(\mathrm{SiCl}_4\) readily undergoes hydrolysis with water because silicon possesses vacant \(3d\) orbitals to accept a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom of a water molecule.

Statement II: Among the crystalline allotropes of carbon, diamond is thermodynamically more stable than graphite, and hence the standard enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\circ\)) of diamond is taken as zero.

Statement III: In the preparation of straight-chain silicones from \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2\mathrm{SiCl}_2\), adding \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) blocks the polymer chain ends and controls the chain length.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle — Hydrolysis of Group 14 Tetrachlorides
Carbon belongs to the second period and lacks \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell, limiting its maximum covalence to four; thus, \(\mathrm{CCl}_4\) cannot accept a lone pair from water and does not undergo hydrolysis. In contrast, silicon belongs to the third period and has vacant \(3d\) orbitals available. Therefore, \(\mathrm{SiCl}_4\) initially accepts a lone pair of electrons from the oxygen atom of water into its vacant \(3d\) orbitals, ultimately forming silicic acid, \(\mathrm{Si(OH)}_4\). Hence, the claim regarding the hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{SiCl}_4\) compared to \(\mathrm{CCl}_4\) is correct.

Step 2: Evaluation — Thermodynamic Stability of Carbon Allotropes
Graphite is thermodynamically the most stable allotrope of carbon, not diamond. Consequently, the standard enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\circ\)) of graphite is taken as zero, whereas \(\Delta_f H^\circ\) of diamond is \(1.90\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) and that of fullerene (\(\mathrm{C}_{60}\)) is \(38.1\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). Hence, the claim that diamond is thermodynamically more stable than graphite with \(\Delta_f H^\circ = 0\) is incorrect.

Step 3: Application — Chain-Length Control in Silicones
Hydrolysis of dimethyldichlorosilane, \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2\mathrm{SiCl}_2\), produces \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2\mathrm{Si(OH)}_2\), which has two reactive \(-\mathrm{OH}\) groups and undergoes condensation polymerisation to form linear silicone chains. When trimethylchlorosilane, \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3\mathrm{SiCl}\), is added, its hydrolysis yields \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3\mathrm{SiOH}\) with only one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group, which condenses at the chain end and prevents further polymerisation, thereby controlling the chain length. Hence, the claim regarding chain termination by \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) is correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding the hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{SiCl}_4\) via vacant \(3d\) orbitals and the chain-length control of silicones using \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3\mathrm{SiCl}\) are correct, whereas the claim regarding the thermodynamic stability and \(\Delta_f H^\circ\) of diamond is incorrect.

answer.text: Only Statement I and Statement II are correct
Only Statement II and Statement III are correct
Only Statement I and Statement III are correct
